On Eid al-Adha the first act is the prayer and the sacrifice comes after returning from it; whoever does so follows the Prophet's way.
A sacrifice slaughtered before the Eid prayer must be repeated, being only meat; the Prophet let Abu Burda offer a young she-goat instead, valid for him alone.
On Eid the prayer comes first and the sacrifice after; an animal slaughtered before the prayer is only meat, and the Prophet allowed Abu Burda alone a young goat instead.
In his Nahr sermon the Prophet said the prayer comes before slaughtering, a sacrifice before it is only meat, and Abu Burda alone could offer a young goat instead.
Going towards Al-Baqi on Eid al-Adha the Prophet said prayer comes before sacrifice, an animal slaughtered earlier is no sacrifice, and allowed one man a young goat for himself alone.
The Prophet slaughtered at the musalla; whoever slaughtered before the prayer was to slaughter again, others in Allah's name, and one man alone was allowed a young goat.
The sacrifice owed for Tamattu, a camel, cow or sheep or else fasting; riding one's sacrificial camel; and the Prophet and Ibn Umar driving sacrificial animals for Hajj with Umrah.

Garlanding and marking sacrificial animals, Aisha twisting their garlands, the Prophet sending them, sheep included, from Medina without entering ihram, riding a sacrificial camel, and giving their skins in charity.
Slaughtering at the Prophet's place at Mina, camels standing, cows for his wives, meat, skins and covers given in charity, none as butcher's wages, and keeping meat past three days.
Ali distributes the saddles and skins of the slaughtered Budn, and Uqba, left with a kid after sharing out sheep, is told to sacrifice it himself.
Aisha twisted garlands for the Prophet's sacrificial animals, which he sent with her father, and nothing lawful became unlawful for him until they were slaughtered.
Given sheep to distribute among the companions for sacrifice, Uqba was told to sacrifice the leftover kid himself.
Seeing a man driving his sacrificial camel, the Prophet told him repeatedly to ride it, adding 'woe to you' when he protested it was for sacrifice.
The Prophet barred keeping sacrifice meat beyond three days only in a year of hunger, so the rich would feed the poor; later it was stored and carried to Medina.
Aqiqa is offered for a newborn boy, with an animal slaughtered and his suffering relieved; Fara' and Atira, the pagans' firstling for idols and the Rajab sheep, are not permitted.
Those who slaughtered their sacrifice before the Eid prayer were told to slaughter another; others were to slaughter after it, mentioning Allah's name.
Sacrifice follows the Eid prayer, earlier slaughter being only meat; Abu Burda and Uqba were allowed young animals, and the Prophet sacrificed two rams, and cows for his wives.
The Prophet slaughtered at the Musalla and sacrificed two horned black-and-white rams himself; a sacrifice before the Eid prayer is repeated, Abu Burda's young goat sufficing for him only.
The Prophet sent garlanded sacrificial animals to the Ka'bah without avoiding anything lawful; sacrificial meat, banned beyond three days in a hard year, was later allowed to be stored.
The Prophet said to eat sacrificial meat for three days, so Ibn Umar, leaving Mina, ate bread with oil rather than the meat of the Hadi.
Seeing a man driving a sacrificial camel, the Prophet told him to ride it, and when he protested it was a Badana, said 'Ride it, woe to you'.
Whoever slaughtered his Eid sacrifice before the prayer was told to slaughter another, and Al-Bara, whose family had done so for a guest, offered a young milch she-goat.
The Prophet slaughtered two rams saying Allah's Name and Allahu Akbar; on the Day of Nahr he told anyone who slaughtered before the prayer to slaughter again.
